newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: OPINION - Ivan Wong comments on Malaysian palm oil.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Ivan Wong comments on Malaysian palm oil.

text.p: KUALA LUMPUR, April 14 - Our final estimate on CPO production in March shows a slight upward revision of 2,000 tonnes to 665,000 tonnes. The increase of 162,000 tonnes or 32 percent over February was largely accounted by Peninsular Malaysia where production rose 31 percent or 117,000 tonnes. The performance of major producers/millers ranged widely from up 20 percent to a staggering 86 percent. Production increases in East Malaysia also ranged widely from 20-60 percent. Some feedback we have on Indonesia suggested a similar pattern.

In February production in Indonesia fell around 20 percent or more severely than the 13 percent drop posted in Malaysia. Our estimate on palm oil stocks at end-March remains unchanged at 725,000 tonnes. Stocks of CPO alone are estimated to have risen 15,000 tonnes to 415,000 tonnes. The entire incrase was accounted by East Malaysia. Stocks of PK/PKO in the country are also estimated to have increased slightly by some 5,000 tonnes to around 140,000 tonnes, oil basis, at end March. With offtake of palm oil and PKO more or less matching output in March, and possibly in April as well, the price undertone for both palm oil and PK/PKO had remained steady to firm in the last two weeks.

The oil palm industry had enjoyed three years of remunerative price in 1994-1996. After recording an all-time high price of 1,472.50 ringgit in 1995. Cash CPO price fell 19 percent to 1,191.50 ringgit in 1996. Price averaged as low as 1,066.50 ringgit in July last year but recovered thereafter to average 1,223 ringgit in December. Although the drop in price last year was an adjustment from the lofty levels registered during August 1995-December 1995, price in 1996 still turned out nearly 100 ringgit better than most plantation budget or trade forecasts.

An analysis of Malaysia's palm oil export performance in 1996 suggested the better than expected price performance was attributed to a fair extent to countries like India, China and Indonesia. Palm oil exports to China (include Hong Kong) had dropped severely by 211,500 tonnes to 1.177 million tonnes in 1995 and there were fears exports would suffer a similar fall in 1996. The final figure shows an increase instead to 1.210 million tonnes.

In the case of India which was the star performance in 1995 when its offtake shot up to 742,400 tonnes from 217,400 tonnes in 1994. Its increase offtake of 284,600 tonnes to 1.027 million tonnes in 1996 was much better than trade forecasts. Indonesia is cited as a contributor because not only there were no exports of CPO to Malaysia during July-December, the country was a sustained buyer of Malaysian palm oil during September-December taking a total of 83,800 tonnes.

Additionally, many smaller importers grouped under "others" made important contribution to Malaysia's good palm oil export performance last year when they collectively raised their offtake by 273,300 tonnes or 39 percent of the total increase in exports of 699,000 tonnes. The price performance of palm oil this year will again be influenced in no small measure by the growth in palm oil exports by China and India.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as necessarily reflecting the views of Reuters).
